q: Bangladesh's national fruit is the ___.
why: Mango gets the poetry and the summer headlines, but kathal gets the title. It is enormous, it smells like a decision, and every part of it gets eaten — seeds roasted, unripe flesh cooked as a vegetable.

q: Bangladesh's national flower is the ___.
why: Shapla grows wild in the flooded fields and ponds that cover much of the country for half the year. It is on the coat of arms, and children still string the stems into necklaces.

q: Bangladesh's national bird is the ___.
why: The doel is small, black-and-white, and startlingly loud for its size. It is on the coins, and Dhaka University's Doel Chattar roundabout is named after it.

q: Bangladesh's national fish is the ___.
why: Ilish is roughly an eighth of the country's fish catch and the centre of an argument that never ends: Padma or Meghna, fried or shorshe. Chandpur calls itself the Ilish capital and nobody has successfully disputed it.

q: Bangladesh's national animal is the ___.
why: It lives in the Sundarbans, and it is why the national cricket team are the Tigers. Counting them is genuinely difficult — the mangrove is tidal, trackless and mostly water.

q: Bangladesh's national tree is the ___ tree.
why: The fruit lost the national title to kathal, but the tree took it instead — a compromise nobody planned. Chapainawabganj and Rajshahi run on mango season the way other places run on harvest.

q: The Sundarbans is generally said to be named after the ___ tree.
why: Sundari is the dominant hardwood of the forest, and the usual reading of the name is 'sundari forest' rather than the tempting 'beautiful forest' — though Bengali being what it is, both meanings sit in the word at once.

q: Bangladesh's only coral island is ___.
why: Locally it is Narikel Jinjira — coconut island. It sits at the far southern tip near the Myanmar coast, and its reef is fragile enough that visitor numbers are now capped.

q: Bangladesh's famously long unbroken sea beach is at ___.
why: Around 120 km of it, which is regularly claimed as the longest natural sea beach in the world. It is named after Hiram Cox, an East India Company officer — one of the more durable pieces of colonial naming left on the map.

q: The town known as Bangladesh's tea capital, home of the seven-layer tea, is ___.
why: Surrounded by tea estates in Moulvibazar district. The seven-layer tea is a genuine local invention — density and sugar content keep the layers from mixing, and the recipe is a closely held secret.

q: The National Parliament building in Dhaka was designed by the architect ___.
why: Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban took over twenty years to build and is widely counted among the great buildings of the twentieth century. Muzharul Islam was offered it first and passed it to Kahn — an act of architectural generosity with few equals.

q: Dhaka's riverside 'Pink Palace' is properly called ___.
why: The residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka on the bank of the Buriganga. The pink is the point — it is visible from the river long before anything else on that bank resolves.

q: The oldest known urban archaeological site in Bangladesh is ___.
why: In Bogura, and the ancient city of Pundranagar. The earliest layers go back well over two thousand years, which puts a city on that spot long before most of the region's better-known capitals existed.

q: Bangladesh's Nobel Peace Prize was awarded for pioneering ___.
why: Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank shared the 2006 prize for small collateral-free loans, lent overwhelmingly to women. The model has been copied, praised and criticised across the world ever since.

q: A cheap oral rehydration formula that has saved tens of millions of lives worldwide was refined and proven in the field in ___.
why: Researchers in Dhaka and Kolkata developed it, and the icddr,b in Dhaka remains a world centre for it. Sugar, salt, water, correct proportions — The Lancet once called it potentially the most important medical advance of the century.

q: The handwoven Dhaka muslin figured fabric on UNESCO's intangible heritage list is ___.
why: Woven on a handloom with no mechanical patterning at all — the motifs are added thread by thread by eye. UNESCO listed it in 2013, and a good sari can take months.

q: In 2023 UNESCO added Dhaka's ___ to its intangible cultural heritage list.
why: The hand-painted tin panels, the film stars, the tigers, the impossible landscapes. Listing it as heritage is slightly funny given the painters were never treated as artists — and entirely deserved.

q: The mystic wandering minstrels of Bengal, recognised by UNESCO, are the ___.
why: Lalon Shah is the towering figure. The songs sit deliberately outside organised religion, which is exactly why they have been loved and distrusted in roughly equal measure for two centuries.

q: The masked dawn procession that opens Pohela Boishakh in Dhaka is called ___.
why: Giant papier-mâché animals, students up all night building them, and a route through Dhaka University. UNESCO listed it in 2016.

q: UNESCO declared 21 February to be International ___ Day.
why: Proposed by Bangladesh and adopted in 1999, marking the date in 1952 when students died over the status of Bengali. It is the rare national commemoration that became a global one.

q: The words of Bangladesh's national anthem were written by ___.
why: 'Amar Sonar Bangla' was written in 1905. Tagore is the only person to have written the national anthem of two countries — India's is his as well.

q: Bangladesh's national poet is ___.
why: The Bidrohi Kobi — the rebel poet. He wrote furious anti-colonial verse and thousands of songs, and he is buried on the Dhaka University campus.

q: The Sixty Dome Mosque, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is at ___.
why: Shat Gombuj Mosque, part of the mosque city of Khalifatabad. The name is a nice piece of folk arithmetic — it does not have sixty domes, and counting them is a standard visitor argument.

q: The great Buddhist monastery ruin of Somapura Mahavihara is at ___.
why: Eighth century, in Naogaon, and one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas. Its plan is thought to have influenced monastery architecture as far away as Southeast Asia.

q: The historic capital of Bengal near Dhaka, famous for muslin, is ___.
why: 'Golden hamlet'. Its abandoned Panam Nagar street of merchant houses is one of the strangest places in the country — a whole colonial-era high street left standing and empty.

q: Bangladesh's national game is ___.
why: Locally Ha-Du-Du. Cricket is what the country actually watches, which makes the official title a small ongoing joke — the national game and the national obsession are not the same sport.

q: The Bangladesh national cricket team is nicknamed the ___.
why: After the Royal Bengal tiger. The team's supporters bring actual tiger costumes to grounds, which has made the nickname unusually literal.

q: The Padma Bridge, opened in 2022, was built primarily with ___.
why: The World Bank withdrew from the project and the government built it anyway. Whatever you think of the politics, the bridge cut a day-long ferry crossing to minutes for the whole southwest.

q: The Dhaka biryani made with raw marinated mutton and rice cooked together in a sealed pot is ___.
why: Kacchi means raw — the meat is not pre-cooked, so the pot has to be judged exactly. It is the default wedding food, and an opinion about the best kacchi in Dhaka is close to mandatory.

q: The dish traditionally eaten on Pohela Boishakh morning is ___ with fried hilsa.
why: Rice soaked in water overnight — historically what you ate because you were poor, now what you queue for on new year's morning. The irony is widely noted and cheerfully ignored.

q: The embroidered quilt made by stitching together old saris is called ___.
why: Nothing is wasted: worn cloth is layered and quilted, and the running stitch becomes the picture. Jasimuddin's poem 'Nakshi Kanthar Math' made it a national symbol.

q: Dried, salted and cured fish, beloved and divisive, is called ___.
why: Chittagong and the coastal districts are the strongholds. It is the one food most likely to get a diaspora household a complaint from the neighbours, and the one most likely to be worth it.

q: The three great rivers whose combined delta forms most of Bangladesh are the Padma, the Jamuna and the ___.
why: The Ganges arrives as the Padma, the Brahmaputra as the Jamuna, and the Meghna carries the combined flow to the sea — one of the largest discharges of fresh water on Earth.

q: The Sylheti language historically had its own script, called ___.
why: Used for centuries for religious and folk texts, largely displaced by Bengali script, and now the subject of a real revival. It has had its own Unicode block since 2005.

q: The largest Indigenous group of the Chittagong Hill Tracts is the ___.
why: The Hill Tracts are home to about a dozen Indigenous peoples with their own languages, and Chakma has its own script descended from the Burmese family. Biju, their new year festival, runs alongside Pohela Boishakh.

q: The sweet that made the town of Muktagacha famous is ___.
why: Bangladesh's sweets are fiercely regional: monda from Muktagacha, chomchom from Porabari, mishti doi from Bogura. Bringing the wrong town's sweet to a wedding is noticed.

q: The everyday Bangladeshi English term for a scheduled power cut is ___.
why: A piece of utility jargon that became ordinary speech. Whole childhoods are structured around it — homework by candle, the fan stopping, and the particular cheer of the whole neighbourhood when it comes back.

q: In Dhaka, a 'CNG' means a ___.
why: Named after the fuel, compressed natural gas, and now simply the name of the vehicle. Caged, green, metered in theory, and negotiated in practice.

q: The dish Bangladeshis famously crave the moment it starts raining is ___.
why: Rice and lentils cooked together, with beef or ilish or just a fried egg. The rain-khichuri connection is close to a national reflex and survives every kind of relocation.

q: The crisp hollow street snack filled with spiced potato and tamarind water is called ___ in Bangladesh.
why: Golgappa and pani puri are the same idea under other names elsewhere — and the differences in filling and sourness are real enough to start an argument at any diaspora gathering.

q: The cash that children collect from elders at Eid is called ___.
why: Crisp new notes, obtained from the bank specially. The rate is set by nothing but reputation, and the accounting done by cousins afterwards is merciless.

q: The turmeric ceremony held before a Bangladeshi wedding is the ___.
why: Literally 'turmeric on the body'. It has quietly become the most-photographed event of the whole wedding, and in the diaspora it is often the one night the entire extended family actually turns up.

q: The reception hosted by the groom's family after a Bangladeshi wedding is called ___.
why: Literally 'bride's rice' — the bride formally serving rice to her new household. In practice it is a very large lunch with a very long queue for the stage photo.

q: London's Banglatown, lined with curry houses and hung with green-and-red arches, is centred on ___.
why: The street has been a first stop for wave after wave of migrants — Huguenot, Jewish, then Bengali. The same building on the corner has been a chapel, a synagogue and a mosque.

q: The London borough with the largest Bangladeshi population is ___.
why: Bangladeshis are the largest single ethnic group in the borough, and it has elected Bangladeshi-origin councillors and mayors for decades. Canary Wharf's towers are in the same borough, which makes the inequality unusually visible.

q: The overwhelming majority of British Bangladeshis trace their origin to the ___ region.
why: It began with Sylheti lascars working the steamship engine rooms out of Kolkata, and chain migration did the rest. It is why Sylheti, not standard Bengali, is the community language of British Banglatown.

q: The first Bengalis to settle in Britain in numbers arrived as ___ on British ships.
why: Sylheti men crewed the boiler rooms of steamships out of Kolkata, and some stepped off in London and stayed. The community is older than most people assume — there were Bengali sailors in the East End in the nineteenth century.

q: The New York neighbourhood that is the centre of Bangladeshi life in the city is ___.
why: Seventy-Third Street and Thirty-Seventh Avenue, sari shops and mishti and a Bangladeshi bookshop. Kensington in Brooklyn is close behind, with its own stretch renamed Little Bangladesh.

q: Chicago's South Asian commercial strip, thick with Bangladeshi and Indian shops, is ___ Avenue.
why: Honorary street signs along it carry both Indian and Bangladeshi names, on the same road, a few blocks apart — a piece of civic diplomacy done entirely in signage.

q: The small Michigan city with a large Bangladeshi community and a Bangladeshi-American majority on its city council is ___.
why: Historically a Polish city entirely surrounded by Detroit, now one of the most immigrant-dense places in America. The stretch along Conant is known as Banglatown.

q: The dish a British Foreign Secretary once called 'a true British national dish' is ___.
why: Robin Cook, in a 2001 speech about multiculturalism. The dish barely exists in South Asia — it was invented for British tastes, in kitchens largely staffed by Sylhetis.

q: For decades, the large majority of Britain's 'Indian' restaurants were actually owned and run by ___.
why: Commonly put at around two-thirds to three-quarters of the trade. 'Indian' was a commercial decision, not a description — it was the word the customers already knew.

q: The first British MP of Bangladeshi origin, elected in 2010, was ___.
why: Elected for Bethnal Green and Bow — the Tower Hamlets seat, which makes the timing look less inevitable than it was: the community had been there for generations before it sent one of its own to Parliament.

q: In diaspora slang, 'ABCD' stands for American Born Confused ___.
why: Affectionate, insulting or self-applied depending entirely on who is saying it. The full joke continues through the alphabet — the rest is rarely remembered and never as good.

q: Across the diaspora, the weekend institution that teaches children Bengali is usually called ___.
why: Usually a rented hall, a volunteer teacher and children who would rather be anywhere else. It is also, quite often, the only reason the next generation can read a Bengali alphabet at all.

q: Money sent home by Bangladeshis working abroad is called ___.
why: One of the largest sources of foreign currency in the country, and Bangladesh is consistently among the world's top receiving nations. Most of it comes from workers in the Gulf, not from the West.

q: The largest number of Bangladeshi migrant workers abroad are in ___.
show: The Gulf (especially Saudi Arabia and the UAE)
why: The Western diaspora is the visible one — the restaurants, the MPs, the students. The far larger migration is to Gulf construction and domestic work, on contracts that rarely lead to settlement.

q: Europe's largest Bengali street festival, held each summer in Tower Hamlets, is the ___.
why: Bengali new year moved outdoors into an East London park, with a crowd that has run into the tens of thousands. The date drifts to fit the British summer, which is its own small act of adaptation.

q: The single most reliable way to cause offence entering a Bangladeshi home anywhere in the world is to keep your ___ on.
why: The pile by the door is the real front door. In colder countries this survives entirely intact, which is why every diaspora hallway has a shoe mountain and a visitor standing on one leg.

q: Any woman of your parents' generation, related to you or not, is addressed as ___.
why: Kinship terms do the work that names do elsewhere. Getting it wrong in either direction — too junior, too senior — is a small social injury that the whole room registers immediately.

q: In 2010 the city of Los Angeles officially designated a neighbourhood called Little ___.
why: A small stretch near Koreatown, and the designation was genuinely contested — the community had to campaign for the signs against a competing claim on the same blocks.

q: In New York City, Bengali became the first ___ language offered on official election ballots.
why: Introduced in Queens under the federal Voting Rights Act, which requires translated ballots once a language group passes a threshold. Bengali got there before Hindi, Urdu or Punjabi.

q: Manchester's 'Curry Mile' runs through the district of ___.
why: A half-mile of Wilmslow Road, neon-lit and mostly South Asian-run. It is the closest thing outside London to Brick Lane, and just as much a student landmark as a community one.

q: The 'Balti Triangle', named after a style of curry served in a pressed steel bowl, is in ___.
why: The balti was invented in Birmingham, not in South Asia — a British dish with a South Asian name, cooked in restaurants largely opened by Pakistani and Bangladeshi families.

q: The Tower Hamlets electoral ward covering Brick Lane is officially named Spitalfields and ___.
why: One of very few places where a diaspora community's own name for its neighbourhood was written into the official map. The street signs run in both English and Bengali.

q: Linguists generally hold that Sylheti and standard Bengali are not fully ___.
why: It matters practically: a British Bangladeshi family needing an interpreter is often badly served by a standard Bengali one, which has caused real problems in hospitals and courts.

q: Italy's largest Bangladeshi community is concentrated in ___.
why: Centred on Torpignattara, to the point that the neighbourhood is nicknamed Banglatown. Italy has one of the largest Bangladeshi populations in Europe after Britain.

q: British students can sit a GCSE, a national school qualification, in the ___ language.
why: A direct consequence of community size. It is also a small annual comedy: the exam is in standard Bengali, and a great many of the candidates grew up speaking Sylheti at home.

q: Monica Ali's 2003 novel about a Bangladeshi woman in London's East End is called ___.
why: Booker-shortlisted, and it caused a genuine argument on the street it was named after — some residents felt it caricatured them. That fight is now part of the book's story.

q: The long collarless shirt a Bangladeshi man wears to Eid is called a ___.
why: Confusingly named after a region nowhere near Bengal, and everywhere else in South Asia the same garment is a kurta. Bought a size large so it survives the year.

q: In the diaspora, Eid prayers are commonly held in a park or a rented ___ because no mosque is big enough.
why: Eid prayer happens once, at one time, and the whole community turns up at once — so the building that fits it is a sports centre with the badminton lines still on the floor.

q: The universal diaspora anxiety before flying home is the airline's ___ allowance.
why: Two suitcases of gifts, weighed on a bathroom scale the night before, repacked twice. Everyone in the family has an opinion and at least one item gets left on the hallway floor.

q: Outside the Gulf, the single largest destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers has been ___.
why: Plantations, factories and construction, on recruitment schemes that have been repeatedly suspended and restarted over allegations of exploitation. Singapore's shipyards are the other large Southeast Asian draw.

q: The Bengali word 'probash', as in the probashi community, means living ___.
why: It carries a faint ache that 'diaspora' does not — the word assumes a home you are away from, which is exactly the argument the second generation tends to have with the first.
